claim: The synaptonemal complex (SC) is a ~100-nm-wide ladder-like meiotic structure present in all eukaryotic clades.
source: The synaptonemal complex (SC) is a ~100-nm-wide ladder-like meiotic structure present in all eukaryotic clades, where it aligns parental chromosomes and regulates exchanges between them.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to electron microscopy studies across multiple organisms.

claim: The SC aligns parental chromosomes and regulates exchanges between them.
source: The synaptonemal complex (SC) is a ~100-nm-wide ladder-like meiotic structure present in all eukaryotic clades, where it aligns parental chromosomes and regulates exchanges between them.
evidence: This functional role is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about SC function.

claim: SC proteins are highly divergent within Caenorhabditis despite conserved ultrastructure and functions.
source: Despite the conserved ultrastructure and functions of the SC, SC proteins are highly divergent within Caenorhabditis.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SC proteins have highly conserved length and coiled-coil domain structure.
source: However, SC proteins have highly conserved length and coiled-coil domain structure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 2.

claim: The same unconventional conservation signature found in Caenorhabditis SC proteins is also present in Drosophila and mammals.
source: We found the same unconventional conservation signature in Drosophila and mammals, and used it to identify a novel SC protein in Pristionchus pacificus, Ppa-SYP-1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through comparative analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Ppa-SYP-1 is a novel SC protein in Pristionchus pacificus identified using the unconventional conservation signature.
source: We found the same unconventional conservation signature in Drosophila and mammals, and used it to identify a novel SC protein in Pristionchus pacificus, Ppa-SYP-1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4.

claim: Coiled-coils play wide-ranging roles in the structure and function of the SC.
source: Our work suggests that coiled-coils play wide-ranging roles in the structure and function of the SC, and more broadly, that expanding sequence analysis beyond measures of per-site similarity can enhance our understanding of protein evolution and function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the conservation analysis and stated in the abstract.

claim: Expanding sequence analysis beyond measures of per-site similarity can enhance understanding of protein evolution and function.
source: Our work suggests that coiled-coils play wide-ranging roles in the structure and function of the SC, and more broadly, that expanding sequence analysis beyond measures of per-site similarity can enhance our understanding of protein evolution and function.
evidence: This is a broader conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: Functionally important protein domains tend to undergo purifying selection and evolve slowly.
source: Often, functionally important domains undergo purifying selection and tend to evolve slowly.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Enzymatic active sites require precise positioning of amino acids and can be identified based on sequence conservation.
source: For example, enzymatic active sites require precise positioning of amino acids and can be identified based on sequence conservation.
evidence: This is stated as an example of conventional protein evolution in the introduction.

claim: Many genes in the immune system are fast-evolving and undergo recurrent changes (positive selection) to uphold tight interaction interfaces with foreign proteins.
source: Many genes in the immune system are fast-evolving and undergo recurrent changes (positive selection) to uphold tight interaction interfaces with foreign proteins (Sawyer et al., 2005; Mitchell et al., 2012; Daugherty and Malik, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations in the introduction.

claim: The SC is present in all eukaryotic clades and is essential for meiosis.
source: The SC is present in all eukaryotic clades and is essential for meiosis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The SC brings parental chromosomes into close proximity in meiotic prophase and forms the interface between them.
source: It brings parental chromosomes into close proximity in meiotic prophase and forms the interface between them.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing SC function.

claim: The SC regulates genetic exchanges (crossovers), which serve as the physical link between parental chromosomes during the first meiotic division.
source: The SC also regulates genetic exchanges (crossovers), which serve as the physical link between parental chromosomes during the first meiotic division.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing SC function.

claim: The SC was first observed more than 60 years ago.
source: First observed more than 60 years ago (Moses, 1956; Fawcett, 1956), the SC is a 100-nm-wide, ladder-like structure with regularly spaced rungs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with citations to the original observations.

claim: The SC is a 100-nm-wide, ladder-like structure with regularly spaced rungs.
source: First observed more than 60 years ago (Moses, 1956; Fawcett, 1956), the SC is a 100-nm-wide, ladder-like structure with regularly spaced rungs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A with electron micrographs.

claim: The ultrastructure of the SC was found to be remarkably conserved across numerous organisms.
source: In the decades since, electron microscopy allowed the characterization of the SC in meiocytes from numerous organisms, where its ultrastructure was found to be remarkably conserved (Gillies and Moens, 2008; Carpenter, 1975; MacQueen et al., 2002; Schmekel et al., 1993; Moses et al., 1977).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: SC proteins are perplexingly divergent and cannot be identified across distant taxa based on sequence homology.
source: The advent of molecular genetics allowed cloning of SC proteins and revealed that they are perplexingly divergent and cannot be identified across distant taxa based on sequence homology.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an established observation.

claim: The components of the axis share clear sequence homology between clades as distant as plants and humans.
source: In contrast, the components of the axis, another meiosis-specific chromosomal structure and the assembly platform for the SC, share clear sequence homology between clades as distant as plants and humans (Rillo-Bohn et al., 2021; Cobbe and Heck, 2004; Aravind and Koonin, 1998).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: All SC proteins are present in the Elegans and Drosophilae supergroups.
source: All SC proteins are present in the Elegans and Drosophilae supergroups, indicating that they have been preserved for over 30 million years (Cutter, 2008; Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SC proteins have been preserved for over 30 million years in Caenorhabditis.
source: All SC proteins are present in the Elegans and Drosophilae supergroups, indicating that they have been preserved for over 30 million years (Cutter, 2008; Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to evolutionary timing.

claim: SC proteins in C. elegans are interdependent for their function.
source: This broad preservation is not surprising given that SC proteins in C. elegans are interdependent for their function and that their elimination causes a dramatic drop in viable progeny (MacQueen et al., 2002; Hurlock et al., 2020; Colaiácovo et al., 2003; Smolikov et al., 2007; Smolikov et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Elimination of SC proteins causes a dramatic drop in viable progeny in C. elegans.
source: This broad preservation is not surprising given that SC proteins in C. elegans are interdependent for their function and that their elimination causes a dramatic drop in viable progeny (MacQueen et al., 2002; Hurlock et al., 2020; Colaiácovo et al., 2003; Smolikov et al., 2007; Smolikov et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: SC protein amino acid percent identity drops rapidly as more distantly related species are included in the comparison.
source: In line with this possibility, SC protein amino acid percent identity drops rapidly as more distantly related species are included in the comparison (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SC proteins are among the most diverged proteins in Caenorhabditis.
source: We found that SC proteins are among the most diverged proteins in Caenorhabditis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: There are significantly more amino acid substitutions per site in SYP-1–SYP-5 compared to the Caenorhabditis proteome.
source: On average, there are significantly more amino acid substitutions per site in SYP-1–SYP-5 compared to the Caenorhabditis proteome (SC proteins: median amino acid substitutions per site = 1.64, other proteins = 0.43, p-value=0.0005, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The median SC amino acid substitutions per site is 1.64, compared to 0.43 for other proteins.
source: On average, there are significantly more amino acid substitutions per site in SYP-1–SYP-5 compared to the Caenorhabditis proteome (SC proteins: median amino acid substitutions per site = 1.64, other proteins = 0.43, p-value=0.0005, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The high divergence of SC proteins cannot be explained by positive selection.
source: The high divergence of SC proteins cannot be explained by positive selection (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by statistical tests in Table 1.

claim: There is no evidence for positive selection in any Caenorhabditis SC protein.
source: However, we found no evidence for positive selection in any Caenorhabditis SC protein (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: Fewer than 50% of sites in SC proteins evolve under purifying selection.
source: Consistent with the high divergence observed above (Figure 1C and D), we found that fewer than 50% of sites evolve under purifying selection when examined on a per-site basis using a Fixed Effects Likelihood model (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Neutral evolution (lack of constraint) explains the high divergence of SC proteins in the Caenorhabditis lineage.
source: Altogether, our analysis indicates that neutral evolution (lack of constraint) explains the high divergence of SC proteins in the Caenorhabditis lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the selection analysis.

claim: SC proteins show striking conservation of the position and length of coiled-coils.
source: These plots reveal striking conservation of the position and length of coiled-coils.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In SYP-1, the coiled-coil begins precisely at position 40 and ends at position 400 in all species.
source: For example, in SYP-1, the coiled-coil begins precisely at position 40 and ends at position 400 in all species (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a specific observation stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Disruptions in coiled-coils are conserved across species.
source: Disruptions, observable as dips in an otherwise continuous coiled-coil, are also conserved (marked by asterisks in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SYP-1 has a short (<10 amino acids) disruption at position 110.
source: SYP-1 has a short (<10 amino acids) disruption at position 110, whereas SYP-3 and SYP-5 have longer disruptions (20–50 amino acids).
evidence: This is a specific observation stated in the text.

claim: SYP-3 and SYP-5 have longer disruptions (20–50 amino acids) in their coiled-coils.
source: SYP-1 has a short (<10 amino acids) disruption at position 110, whereas SYP-3 and SYP-5 have longer disruptions (20–50 amino acids).
evidence: This is a specific observation stated in the text.

claim: Disruptions in coiled-coils might create bends in the otherwise rod-like structure of SC proteins.
source: These disruptions might create bends in the otherwise rod-like structure of SC proteins (Dunce et al., 2018), similar to the conserved 'kinks' and 'elbows' in the coiled-coils of the kinetochore protein NDC80 (Maure et al., 2011; Hsu and Toda, 2011) and the ring-like SMC-family proteins (Yatskevich et al., 2019; Beasley et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with supporting citations to similar phenomena in other proteins.

claim: SC proteins have a significantly higher coiled-coil conservation score on average compared to all other proteins.
source: Consistent with our qualitative observations, SC proteins have a significantly higher coiled-coil conservation scores on average compared to all other proteins (Figure 2B; median coiled-coil conservation score for SC proteins = 0.56, other = 0.12, p-value=0.00019) and compared to other coiled-coil proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The median coiled-coil conservation score for SC proteins is 0.56, compared to 0.12 for other proteins.
source: Consistent with our qualitative observations, SC proteins have a significantly higher coiled-coil conservation scores on average compared to all other proteins (Figure 2B; median coiled-coil conservation score for SC proteins = 0.56, other = 0.12, p-value=0.00019) and compared to other coiled-coil proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neither coiled-coils nor their edges leave discernible signatures of sequence conservation on SC proteins.
source: Neither coiled-coils nor their edges leave discernible signatures of sequence conservation on SC proteins (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is no strong correlation between the coiled-coils and amino acids under purifying selection.
source: We also do not find strong correlation between the coiled-coils and amino acids under purifying selection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The coiled-coil conservation score is more informative than a binary measure of coiled-coil domain prediction.
source: More broadly, this result suggests that the coiled-coil conservation score is more informative than a binary measure of coiled-coil domain prediction (i.e., presence/absence of coiled-coil).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the analysis.

claim: The median variation in length of SC proteins is significantly lower than that of other Caenorhabditis proteins.
source: We found that the median variation in length of SC proteins is significantly lower than that of other Caenorhabditis proteins (Figure 2C, median coefficient of variation of protein length for SC proteins = 0.03, other = 0.16, p-value=0.0004), again, in striking contrast to their diverged primary amino acid sequence (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The median coefficient of variation of protein length for SC proteins is 0.03, compared to 0.16 for other proteins.
source: We found that the median variation in length of SC proteins is significantly lower than that of other Caenorhabditis proteins (Figure 2C, median coefficient of variation of protein length for SC proteins = 0.03, other = 0.16, p-value=0.0004), again, in striking contrast to their diverged primary amino acid sequence (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a significant depletion of indels in the coiled-coils of SC proteins compared with regions outside the coiled-coils.
source: Indeed, we find a significant depletion of indels in the coiled-coils of SC proteins compared with regions outside the coiled-coils (Figure 2D, Table 2; two-tailed p-value from Fisher's test comparing alignment positions with indels to alignment positions that are part of coiled-coils < 0.0001).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2D and Table 2.

claim: Significant depletion of indels was detected in the coiled-coils of SYP-1, -4, and -5.
source: When examined individually, we detected significant depletion of indels in the coiled-coils of SYP-1, -4, and -5 (Table 2; SYP-2 and SYP-3 had only two indels each, preventing statistical analysis).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 2.

claim: Selection acts against indels in the coiled-coils of the SC.
source: In summary, selection acts against indels in the coiled-coils of the SC, consistent with the conservation of SC protein length and domain arrangement.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the indel analysis.

claim: The three known Drosophila SC proteins exhibit a similar evolutionary signature to SC proteins in Caenorhabditis.
source: In a dataset of 30 Drosophila species spanning 40 million years of evolution, the three known Drosophila SC proteins – Corolla, Corona, and the transverse filament protein C(3)G – exhibit a similar evolutionary signature to SC proteins in Caenorhabditis, and likewise, occupy a region of the coordinate system occupied by few other proteins (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mammalian SC proteins exhibited conserved coiled-coil domains.
source: While mammalian SC proteins exhibited conserved coiled-coil domains (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4), they had a lower overall divergence compared to Caenorhabditis and Drosophila SC proteins (median amino acid substitutions per site for mammalian SC proteins = 0.26 compared to 1.64 in Caenorhabditis and 1.69 in Drosophila).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Mammalian SC proteins had a lower overall divergence compared to Caenorhabditis and Drosophila SC proteins.
source: While mammalian SC proteins exhibited conserved coiled-coil domains (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4), they had a lower overall divergence compared to Caenorhabditis and Drosophila SC proteins (median amino acid substitutions per site for mammalian SC proteins = 0.26 compared to 1.64 in Caenorhabditis and 1.69 in Drosophila).
evidence: This is stated in the results with specific quantitative values.

claim: The median amino acid substitutions per site for mammalian SC proteins is 0.26 compared to 1.64 in Caenorhabditis and 1.69 in Drosophila.
source: While mammalian SC proteins exhibited conserved coiled-coil domains (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4), they had a lower overall divergence compared to Caenorhabditis and Drosophila SC proteins (median amino acid substitutions per site for mammalian SC proteins = 0.26 compared to 1.64 in Caenorhabditis and 1.69 in Drosophila).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result stated in the text.

claim: The lower divergence of mammalian SC proteins might be explained by the overall lower median divergence of the proteome along the mammalian lineage.
source: This might be explained by the overall lower median divergence of the proteome along the mammalian lineage (median amino acid substitution per site for all mammalian proteins = 0.068 compared to 0.43 in Caenorhabditis and 0.27 in Drosophila).
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation with supporting data.

claim: Ppa-SYP-1 is a transverse filament protein arranged in a head-to-head orientation, spanning the width of the SC.
source: This indicates that Ppa-SYP-1 is a transverse filament protein arranged in a head-to-head orientation, spanning the width of the SC.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on imaging data in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Ppa-SYP-1 appears to be a functional homolog of C. elegans SYP-1.
source: Ppa-SYP-1 appears to be a functional homolog of C. elegans SYP-1: they are both transverse filament proteins that contain similar coiled-coil domain structures, predicted to be 55 and 51 nm long, respectively (Figure 4I, compare to Figure 2A, SYP-1; Tung and Roeder, 1998; Steinert et al., 1993), and both harbor Polo-Box Domains in their C-termini (STP at positions 451–453 for C. elegans SYP-1 [Sato-Carlton et al., 2018] and positions 658–660 and 681–683 for Ppa-SYP-1).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting structural and functional comparisons.

claim: Ppa-SYP-1 has no significant homology to C. elegans SYP-1, or to any known SC protein.
source: This is despite the fact that Ppa-SYP-1 has no significant homology to C. elegans SYP-1, or, for that matter, to any known SC protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: SC proteins provide a clear example of a first-order amino acid fitness landscape tolerant of mutations accompanied by second-order fitness landscapes that impose strong evolutionary constraints.
source: SC proteins thus provide a clear example of a first-order amino acid fitness landscape tolerant of mutations accompanied by second-order fitness landscapes (properties derived from primary amino acid sequence) that impose strong evolutionary constraints.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study's findings.

claim: The evolutionary constraints acting on SC proteins appear to be distinct from constraints imposed on other meiotic proteins.
source: The evolutionary constraints acting on SC proteins appear to be distinct from constraints imposed on other meiotic proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the comparative analysis.

claim: The proteins that make up the meiotic axis are recognizable by sequence homology across all eukaryotic clades.
source: For example, the proteins that make up the meiotic axis, which acts as the assembly scaffold for the SC and includes the cohesin complex and meiotic HORMA domain proteins (HORMAD1 and HORMAD2 in mammals, HTP-1/2, HTP-3 and HIM-3 in C. elegans), are recognizable by sequence homology across all eukaryotic clades (Cobbe and Heck, 2004; Aravind and Koonin, 1998; van Hooff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In the SC, the strong selection acting on coiled-coils likely reflects biophysical and structural properties that are conserved across phyla.
source: In the SC, the strong selection acting on coiled-coils likely reflects biophysical and structural properties that are conserved across phyla.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the discussion.

claim: Coiled-coils in transverse filament proteins help determine the 100 nm space between the parental chromosomes.
source: Coiled-coils in transverse filament proteins help determine the 100 nm space between the parental chromosomes (Sym and Roeder, 1995; Billmyre et al., 2019; Ollinger et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The specific arrangement of the coiled-coils and their disruptions might determine other aspects of the 3D architecture of the SC lattice.
source: An attractive hypothesis is that the specific arrangement of the coiled-coils and their disruptions determines other aspects of the 3D architecture of the SC lattice (Dunce et al., 2018), such as its axial depth or the uniform lateral spacing between the ladder rungs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The SC in worms, flies, and yeast has been shown to assemble through phase-separation.
source: Despite its ordered appearance, the SC in worms, flies, and yeast has recently been shown to assemble through phase-separation (also referred to as condensation; Rog et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Coiled-coils can facilitate phase-separation.
source: Coiled-coils can facilitate phase-separation (Schmidt and Görlich, 2015; Li et al., 2012), potentially by promoting multivalent interactions (Newton et al., 2021; Mitrea and Kriwacki, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: SPD-5 has been shown to promote microtubule nucleation in mitosis through condensation.
source: Tellingly, SPD-5, which shares an evolutionary signature with SC proteins in Caenorhabditis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), has been shown to promote microtubule nucleation in mitosis through condensation (Woodruff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Indels and substitutions typically occur together.
source: Such uncoupling is unusual since indels and substitutions typically occur together (Tóth-Petróczy and Tawfik, 2013; Leushkin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: When manually annotating the dataset of SC proteins in Caenorhabditis, annotation errors were corrected in 18% of sequences.
source: When manually annotating our dataset of SC proteins in Caenorhabditis, we corrected annotation errors in 18% of sequences, most of which would have been otherwise mistakenly scored as alterations to protein lengths (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion describing the manual curation process.

claim: The C-terminus of Ppa-SYP-1 formed parallel tracks spaced 114 nm apart on average.
source: Its C-terminus formed parallel tracks spaced 114 nm apart on average, whereas the N-terminus formed a single, narrower track (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: The N-terminus of Ppa-SYP-1 formed a single, narrower track.
source: Its C-terminus formed parallel tracks spaced 114 nm apart on average, whereas the N-terminus formed a single, narrower track (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Almost all chromosomes in Ppa-syp-1 mutants lacked crossovers.
source: Examination of condensed meiotic chromosomes (DAPI bodies) revealed that almost all chromosomes in Ppa-syp-1 lacked crossovers (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ppa-syp-1 mutant hermaphrodites give rise to almost no viable self-progeny.
source: Consistent with this, Ppa-syp-1 mutant hermaphrodites give rise to almost no viable self-progeny; a reflection of embryonic aneuploidy caused by uncoordinated meiotic chromosome segregation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The SC was first observed by Moses in 1956.
source: First observed more than 60 years ago (Moses, 1956; Fawcett, 1956), the SC is a 100-nm-wide, ladder-like structure with regularly spaced rungs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the original observation.

claim: The SC was first observed by Fawcett in 1956.
source: First observed more than 60 years ago (Moses, 1956; Fawcett, 1956), the SC is a 100-nm-wide, ladder-like structure with regularly spaced rungs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the original observation.

claim: Six SC proteins have been identified in C. elegans: SYP-1–SYP-6.
source: In the model organism Caenorhabditis elegans, six SC proteins have been identified: SYP-1–SYP-6 (MacQueen et al., 2002; Hurlock et al., 2020; Colaiácovo et al., 2003; Smolikov et al., 2007; Smolikov et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: SYP-1, SYP-5, and SYP-6 are transverse filament proteins.
source: SYP-1, SYP-5, and the C. elegans -specific SYP-5 paralog, SYP-6, are transverse filament proteins (MacQueen et al., 2002; Hurlock et al., 2020; Colaiácovo et al., 2003; Schild-Prüfert et al., 2011; Köhler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: SYP-6 is a C. elegans-specific SYP-5 paralog.
source: SYP-1, SYP-5, and the C. elegans -specific SYP-5 paralog, SYP-6, are transverse filament proteins (MacQueen et al., 2002; Hurlock et al., 2020; Colaiácovo et al., 2003; Schild-Prüfert et al., 2011; Köhler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: Three instances of protein duplication were found in Caenorhabditis SC proteins.
source: In addition, we found three instances of protein duplication; the previously identified paralogs SYP-5 and SYP-6 in C. elegans (Hurlock et al., 2020), a SYP-1 duplication in Caenorhabditis panamensis and a SYP-2 duplication in the common ancestor of Caenorhabditis nouraguensis and Caenorhabditis becei (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B and supplements.

claim: A SYP-1 duplication occurred in Caenorhabditis panamensis.
source: In addition, we found three instances of protein duplication; the previously identified paralogs SYP-5 and SYP-6 in C. elegans (Hurlock et al., 2020), a SYP-1 duplication in Caenorhabditis panamensis and a SYP-2 duplication in the common ancestor of Caenorhabditis nouraguensis and Caenorhabditis becei (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B and supplements.

claim: A SYP-2 duplication occurred in the common ancestor of Caenorhabditis nouraguensis and Caenorhabditis becei.
source: In addition, we found three instances of protein duplication; the previously identified paralogs SYP-5 and SYP-6 in C. elegans (Hurlock et al., 2020), a SYP-1 duplication in Caenorhabditis panamensis and a SYP-2 duplication in the common ancestor of Caenorhabditis nouraguensis and Caenorhabditis becei (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B and supplements.

claim: SYP-3, -4, and -5 orthologs were identified in both C. plicata and C. monodelphis.
source: This allowed us to identify SYP-3, -4, and -5 orthologs in both C. plicata and C. monodelphis (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B and supplement.

claim: SYP-2 was found in C. plicata but not in C. monodelphis.
source: We also found SYP-2 in C. plicata but not in C. monodelphis.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: SYP-1 was not identified in either C. plicata or C. monodelphis.
source: We were unable to identify SYP-1 in either C. plicata or C. monodelphis (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B and supplement.

claim: Drosophila SC proteins were not found in other insects.
source: Drosophila SC proteins were not found in other insects (Hemmer and Blumenstiel, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Among vertebrates, sequence similarity of the transverse filament protein SYCP1 is limited to two short motifs.
source: Among vertebrates, sequence similarity of the transverse filament protein SYCP1 is limited to two short motifs, which are absent in Caenorhabditis and Drosophila (Fraune et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: The two short conserved motifs in SYCP1 are absent in Caenorhabditis and Drosophila.
source: Among vertebrates, sequence similarity of the transverse filament protein SYCP1 is limited to two short motifs, which are absent in Caenorhabditis and Drosophila (Fraune et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Ppa-SYP-4 has been identified based on limited sequence similarity to the C-terminus of C. elegans SYP-4.
source: One SC protein, Ppa-SYP-4, has been identified based on a limited sequence similarity to the C-terminus of C. elegans SYP-4 (Rillo-Bohn et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Ppa-SYP-4's coiled-coil is predicted to be only 31 nm long, too short to span the 100 nm SC as a head-to-head dimer.
source: Notably, Ppa-SYP-4's coiled-coil is predicted to be only 31 nm long, too short to span the 100 nm SC as a head-to-head dimer, suggesting that we have yet to identify a transverse filament protein in P. pacificus.
evidence: This is stated in the results with an inference about the need for another transverse filament protein.

claim: Eight candidate SC proteins were identified in Pristionchus after filtering.
source: We further filtered our list for germline enriched genes (see Materials and methods) and were left with only eight candidate SC proteins, one of which was, gratifyingly, Ppa-SYP-4.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the bioinformatics pipeline.

claim: Ppa-SYP-4 was among the eight candidate SC proteins identified in Pristionchus.
source: We further filtered our list for germline enriched genes (see Materials and methods) and were left with only eight candidate SC proteins, one of which was, gratifyingly, Ppa-SYP-4.
evidence: This is stated in the results as validation of the approach.

claim: Null alleles were generated in the top three candidate SC proteins in Pristionchus using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: We generated null alleles in our top three candidates using CRISPR/Cas9 and found that one of these genes, PPA16075, is an SC protein that we named Ppa-SYP-1.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the experimental approach.

claim: PPA16075 is an SC protein named Ppa-SYP-1.
source: We generated null alleles in our top three candidates using CRISPR/Cas9 and found that one of these genes, PPA16075, is an SC protein that we named Ppa-SYP-1.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: Neither PPA10754 nor PPA35551 exhibited meiotic phenotypes.
source: Neither of the other two candidates (PPA10754 and PPA35551) exhibited meiotic phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: C. elegans SYP-1 contains a Polo-Box Domain at positions 451-453.
source: Ppa-SYP-1 appears to be a functional homolog of C. elegans SYP-1: they are both transverse filament proteins that contain similar coiled-coil domain structures, predicted to be 55 and 51 nm long, respectively (Figure 4I, compare to Figure 2A, SYP-1; Tung and Roeder, 1998; Steinert et al., 1993), and both harbor Polo-Box Domains in their C-termini (STP at positions 451–453 for C. elegans SYP-1 [Sato-Carlton et al., 2018] and positions 658–660 and 681–683 for Ppa-SYP-1).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: The electron micrographs demonstrate the conserved organization and dimensions of the SC across nematode, mouse, and beetles.
source: Right: electron micrographs of the SC from nematode (C. elegans), mouse (M. musculus), and beetles (B. cribrosa), demonstrating the conserved organization and dimensions of the SC.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A and shown in the electron micrographs.

claim: SC proteins assume a stereotypical head-to-head orientation spanning the space between the parental chromosomes with N-termini pointing toward the center of the SC and C-termini pointing outward.
source: Despite poor per-site identity, in cases where SC proteins have been cloned at least one assumes a stereotypical head-to-head orientation spanning the space between the parental chromosomes: N-termini pointing toward the center of the SC and C-termini pointing outward (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: SC proteins with head-to-head orientation are referred to as 'transverse filaments'.
source: SC proteins with this orientation are referred to as 'transverse filaments' and help determine the width of the SC via a central coiled-coil domain (Sym and Roeder, 1995; Tung and Roeder, 1998; Billmyre et al., 2019; Ollinger et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.
